title: The communication plan
blurb: List what a communication plan contains and decode any plan entry into who, what, why, when, how, who sends and feedback.
question: A housing project's communication plan contains the entry: 'Monthly highlight report to the project board by email, issued by the project manager, to support stage decisions; questions taken at the board meeting.' Which contents of a communication plan does this single entry cover?

teach.body: A communication plan sets out how information will be exchanged with the project's stakeholders: WHO needs it, WHAT they need, WHY, WHEN and how often, HOW it will be sent, WHO is responsible for sending it, and how FEEDBACK will be gathered. It is built from the stakeholder analysis and forms part of the project management plan. In plain English: it is the project's 'who hears what, when and how' timetable.

teach.caption: Learn these seven. Exam stems give you a plan entry and ask which one it defines.

teach.loop: Review and update as stakeholders change

head: Who
What & why

teach.caption: A real plan adds a feedback column: how each audience can respond or raise questions.

root.label: One plan entry
root.sub: Monthly highlight report to the board by email, from the PM

teach.body: Leon's stakeholder analysis shows the council planning team has high influence but little interest in weekly detail, while residents are highly interested but have little influence. So the plan gives the council a brief monthly summary by email from Leon, and residents a printed newsletter every fortnight from the community liaison officer, with a phone number and drop-in sessions for questions. When a new housing association joins mid-project, Leon adds them to the plan.

teach.h: In the plan, or somewhere else?

rows.label: Detailed cost of each work package

teach.text: Two classic traps. 1) Detail that belongs in another document (risk scores, task durations, costs) offered as plan content. 2) The plan as a RECORD of what has been sent: it is a plan of what WILL be communicated. And note 'when' includes how often: 'weekly' and 'every Friday' both define timing and frequency.

teach.body: Stakeholders come and go, and their needs change as the project moves through its life cycle. The project manager reviews the communication plan and updates it: adding new stakeholders, changing frequency or method when feedback shows something isn't working, and dropping messages nobody needs.

items: Contents: who (audience), what (message), why (purpose), when and how often, how (method, medium, format), who sends, feedback.
Built from the stakeholder analysis; part of the project management plan.
Not the place for risk scores, durations or costs.
Reviewed and updated as stakeholders and needs change.

summary: You can now outline the contents of a communication plan (who, what, why, when and how often, how, who sends, feedback), decode any plan entry into those parts, and reject content that belongs in other project documents.

A.q: Which of the following would typically be included in a communication plan?
options: The probability score of each risk
The frequency of each communication
The duration of each scheduled task
The cost of each work package
A.why: How often each message is sent (timing and frequency) is a core part of a communication plan.

whyNot.0: Risk scores belong in the risk register.
whyNot.2: Task durations belong in the schedule.
whyNot.3: Work package costs belong in the budget or cost breakdown.

A.q: A communication plan entry says the site update is issued 'every Friday by 12:00'. Which content does this define?
options: The audience for the update
The method used to send it
The timing and frequency
The purpose of the update
A.why: 'Every Friday by 12:00' tells you when and how often the update goes out.

whyNot.0: The audience would be a person or group, such as the sponsor.
whyNot.1: The method would be a channel, such as email or a meeting.
whyNot.3: The purpose would explain why it is sent, such as to inform decisions.

A.q: Which analysis should a project manager mainly draw on to produce a communication plan?
options: Stakeholder analysis
Critical path analysis
Earned value analysis
Investment appraisal
A.why: Stakeholder analysis identifies who the stakeholders are, their interest, influence and needs, which is exactly what the plan is built on.

whyNot.1: Critical path analysis is a scheduling technique.
whyNot.2: Earned value analysis measures cost and schedule performance.
whyNot.3: Investment appraisal supports the business case.

B.q: A plan entry states that the weekly report is 'issued by the project coordinator'. Which content of the plan does this define?
options: The audience
The purpose
The method
The sender
B.why: Naming who issues a communication defines responsibility for sending it.

whyNot.0: The audience is who receives the report, not who issues it.
whyNot.1: The purpose is why the report is sent.
whyNot.2: The method is how it is sent, such as email.

B.q: Which of the following would you LEAST expect to find in a communication plan?
options: The method for each message
The audience for each message
The float on each activity
The purpose of each message
B.why: Float is a scheduling concept found in the schedule or network diagram, not the communication plan.

whyNot.0: Method (how) is a core content of the plan.
whyNot.1: Audience (who) is a core content of the plan.
whyNot.3: Purpose (why) is a core content of the plan.

B.q: A plan entry reads: 'To keep the funding body confident in progress'. Which content of the plan is this?
options: The purpose
The frequency
The sender
The feedback route
B.why: It explains WHY the message is sent, which is its purpose.

whyNot.1: Frequency would be a timing such as monthly.
whyNot.2: The sender would be a named person or role.
whyNot.3: A feedback route would describe how the audience responds.

C.q: A draft plan lists each audience, message, purpose, method, timing and sender. What further content should be added?
options: A log of messages already sent
How feedback will be gathered
The risk owner for each risk
The scope of each deliverable
C.why: Feedback mechanisms let the project manager check messages are understood and the plan is working.

whyNot.0: The plan sets out future communication; a log of sent messages is a record, not plan content.
whyNot.2: Risk owners belong in the risk register.
whyNot.3: Deliverable scope belongs in the scope documents.

C.q: Which THREE are contents of a communication plan? 1) The audience. 2) The method. 3) The risk response. 4) The frequency.
options: 1, 2 and 3
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
1, 2 and 4
C.why: Audience (who), method (how) and frequency (when and how often) are all communication plan contents.

whyNot.0: Risk responses belong in the risk register, not the communication plan.
whyNot.1: Risk responses are not plan content, and the method is missing.
whyNot.2: Risk responses are not plan content, and the audience is missing.

C.q: Midway through delivery, a regulator is identified as a new stakeholder. What should the project manager do with the communication plan?
options: Leave it, as it was fixed at the start
Update it to include the regulator
Copy the regulator into all messages
Replace it with the risk register
C.why: The plan is a living document: new stakeholders are added with their own needs, method, timing and sender.

whyNot.0: The plan is reviewed and updated as stakeholders change.
whyNot.2: Sending everything to everyone causes overload; needs should be planned.
whyNot.3: The risk register has a different purpose and does not plan communication.

reteach.title: Planning a kitchen refit with the family
reteach.question: You are having your kitchen refitted over three weeks. Who needs to hear what, when and how? That is a communication plan.

blocks.body: Your partner needs the daily progress (what) to plan meals (why), every evening (when), over dinner (how), from you (sender). The neighbours need a note through the door (how) a week before the skip arrives (when), to avoid parking rows (why). The fitter needs any changes (what) by text (how) as soon as you decide (when). And each of them can tell you if it's not working: that's feedback.

blocks.text: Notice what is NOT in it: the price of the worktops or the fitting schedule. Those live in other plans. A communication plan only covers communication.

explain.body: WHO: the audiences, taken from the stakeholder analysis (sponsor, board, users, suppliers, the public). WHAT: the information or message each one needs, such as a highlight report or a works notice.

test.q: In a communication plan, what does 'who' refer to?
options: The audiences that need the information
The approver of the project budget
The owner of each project risk
The supplier of each work package
test.why: 'Who' is the audience: the stakeholders who need to receive each communication.

whyNot.1: Budget approval is a governance role, not a plan content.
whyNot.2: Risk owners are recorded in the risk register.
whyNot.3: Suppliers may be an audience, but 'who' means all audiences, not suppliers of work.

explain.body: WHY: the purpose of each message (to inform, to get a decision, to reassure, to coordinate). WHEN: the timing and frequency, such as weekly, at each stage gate or two weeks before works.

test.q: Why does a communication plan record the purpose of each message?
options: So that messages are sent more often
So the risk register can be shortened
So each message has a clear reason
So no feedback needs to be collected
test.why: Recording why each message is sent keeps it focused and avoids communication that serves no purpose.

whyNot.0: Purpose may reduce messages; it does not exist to increase them.
whyNot.1: The risk register is unaffected by the communication plan.
whyNot.3: Feedback is still needed to check messages are understood.

explain.body: HOW: the method, medium or channel and the format (email, meeting, letter, video call, dashboard). WHO SENDS: the person responsible for issuing each communication, so nothing falls between two people.

items.label: email, meeting, letter, video call, notice
the named role that issues it

test.q: Which pairing of plan content and meaning is correct?
options: Who sends: the audience receiving it
When: the reason for sending it
Why: the format of the report
How: the channel, such as email
test.why: 'How' is the method, medium or channel, such as email, a meeting or a letter.

whyNot.0: Who sends is the person responsible for issuing it, not the audience.
whyNot.1: When is timing and frequency; the reason is 'why'.
whyNot.2: Why is the purpose; the format falls under 'how'.

explain.body: FEEDBACK mechanisms let audiences respond and let the project manager check understanding: surveys, Q&A sessions, reply routes, drop-ins. Feedback also shows when the plan needs updating.

test.q: Which of the following is an example of a feedback mechanism in a communication plan?
options: A list of every stakeholder group
A short survey after each update
A deadline for the monthly report
The name of the report's sender
test.why: A survey gathers the audience's response, showing whether messages are understood and useful.

whyNot.0: A stakeholder list defines the audience, not feedback.
